title: The Committee of 1184
text:
In the winter of 1184 the Azure Cloud Sect convened a seven-person committee to read a single shelf of the Library and decide, of each scroll on it, whether to keep, to burn, or to seal. They were to sit three days. They sat eleven. On the eleventh morning the committee-room door was opened by a younger librarian who had brought tea; the tea was returned to the kitchen. The shelf-room was locked from within, a wooden peg driven through the inner latch. A notice had been nailed to the outer door, in the hand of the chief archivist: 'The reading is done. The decision is this peg.'

No one on the committee left the room alive. The sect buried them with full rites and without explanation. The peg was not pulled. The shelf — the west shelf of the third hall — has been closed for eight hundred and forty-two years.

The catalogue Librarian Zhao carries still records the committee's seven names. He has never read them aloud. He will tell you, if pressed, that he does not believe the names are the point. The peg is the point. The sentence is: 'The decision is this peg.' Everything else is footnote.

title: Marginalia to the Sutra of Empty Sleeves
text:
In a hand that is not the hand of the sutra's original scribe, running in thin red ink along the outer margin of every folio:

  *The sleeve is empty because the arm has been given elsewhere.*
  *The word in dust is not 'forget'; it is 'again'.*
  *A student who has read this page has already broken its first teaching. The second teaching is: this is permitted.*
  *The seventh of us believes the sutra teaches the opposite of what it says. The seventh of us is correct. We will keep the sutra anyway. Who are we to read a thing by what it intends?*

The ink is the same red the sect now uses only for death-registers. The marginalia is signed, once, at the end of the last folio, in a character that is not a name but a small drawing: seven strokes, the central one broken.

title: Why Zhao Keeps the Lamps Lit After Closing
text:
Before he was librarian, Zhao was a junior archivist at the Jade-Brush Pavilion in the imperial capital. His son, six years old, would wait each evening at the gate of the pavilion until his father finished the day's cataloguing and walked him home through the lamp-streets. One winter evening — the pavilion's lamps ran late; a visiting official had ordered every chronicle of the Fourth Dynasty brought down — Zhao finished well after dark and found the boy gone. He was told, afterwards, by a neighbour, that the child had gone home alone when the lamps did not come on at the usual time, because he did not wish his mother to worry. He was struck by a palanquin at the Twelfth Street crossing. He did not survive the night.

Zhao resigned the next morning. The Azure Cloud charter, which is older than any emperor, does not require the lamps to be lit at all. Zhao lights them anyway — every evening, before the catalogue, before the tea, before his own reading. The west reading-room's kettle is always warm. He has never said why, in all the years he has been here, and no one has ever asked.

title: The Sword Calamity — An Abridgment
text:
Three hundred and twelve years ago, at a place the annals now refuse to name, nine sword-sects stood against seven demonic ones for reasons that were, at the time, of surpassing moral clarity. None of the nine survived intact. Four of the seven did not survive at all. The surviving three, by common understanding, are: the Scarlet Lotus Pavilion (which does not dispute the understanding), the Blood Moon Cult (which holds that it alone survived the day whole), and a sect whose name is struck from every register the Azure Cloud maintains.

The Azure Cloud lost its first three generations of inner disciples in one afternoon. The Five Poisons Sect, which was neutral but present, is said to have carried the wounded of both sides off the field and been cursed for it by both. The Jadestep Sect was not there; they were hunting a tiger, and the world has since known what became of them.

The abridgment ends with a single sentence in the original hand: 'We write this short because the long version has not yet forgiven us.'

title: The Gatekeeper's Oath
text:
Spoken at the base of the Azure Cloud gate by every gatekeeper-candidate on the morning of the trial. The oath is short. It has not been revised since the founding; it is said to have been written before the sect's charter, and to have been the reason for the charter:

  *To the stranger: I am the first face of my sect.*
  *To my sect: I am the last face of the stranger.*
  *I will not turn a guest without a reason. I will not turn a reason without a guest. I will not be swayed by weather or by gold; by weather, because it always turns; by gold, because it never does.*
  *If I fail the gate, let the gate fail gently — only my watch, and only this once.*

It is traditional for the candidate to practise the knot of their sash for a long time, alone, the night before. No one has ever asked why. Every gatekeeper, it seems, already knows.

title: The West Reading-Room
text:
Off the main library hall, behind a curtain of dark blue felt that has faded in the sun to the colour of old sky, lies the west reading-room. It is not on the charter. No archivist made it. The west wall of the library simply bends at an angle no architect drew, and a small room exists where there should be nothing, with one shuttered window that faces west and one low table that fits exactly one kettle, one cup, one book. The cushion has the shape of a reader's knees pressed into it over what must be centuries.

If you are invited by Librarian Zhao to the west reading-room, you will understand that you have been trusted — not with any secret the library holds, but with the simpler and older thing: the right to sit where it is quiet, and read. The kettle will be warm. The cup will be full. A second cushion will be set out, even when you are alone. It is not Zhao's cushion. He has never said whose it is.
